about.title: A training library, built by a runner, for runners
about.description: Zoned brings together zone-based workouts, training plans, and practical tools. The goal: make training science accessible — no subscription, no tracking, no fluff.

personal.title: The project
personal.bio: Zoned is built by a passionate runner, in the open. The project was born from the need for a simple, zone-based tool to structure training without depending on any proprietary platform.

openSource.title: Open source
openSource.contributions: The code is public on GitHub. Bugs, suggestions, and contributions are welcome.

vibeCoded.title: Built with Claude
vibeCoded.claude: A large part of the code is co-written with Claude (Anthropic). AI is a tool, not a substitute for human judgement on athletic relevance.

privacy.title: Privacy
privacy.noServer: No server, no account, no tracker. Your data stays in your browser.

methodology.title: Methodology
methodology.seoDescription: Zoned's 6-zone model: what it measures, what it doesn't claim, and the published research behind every pace guideline.
methodology.heading:
Six zones,
one scale
methodology.intro: Only one thing is coloured in Zoned: intensity. These six zones split the continuum from very easy jogging to sprinting, and give a common unit to every session, plan and calculator.
methodology.notMeasuredTitle: What Zoned doesn't make the zones say
notMeasured: They don't measure your lactate: they're pace guidelines.
They don't replace how you feel on a tired day.
They vary by a few seconds from one model to the next: Zoned owns its choice and says so.
methodology.scaleCaption: Scale in % of VMA · each block's width is the zone's own width.
methodology.scaleNote: The pace ranges below target the core of each zone: they deliberately leave a margin between two zones.
methodology.noVma: Calculate your VMA to see your personal pace
methodology.threeWaysTitle: Three ways to target a zone
methodology.wayPaceDesc: The most precise on flat ground, thrown off by hills and strong wind.
methodology.wayHrDesc: Robust, but lags the effort by 30 to 60 seconds.
methodology.wayFeelDesc: Always available, and the only one that accounts for today's fatigue.
methodology.zonedChoiceText: Six zones rather than five or three: five doesn't distinguish pure speed from VMA pace, three isn't enough to write concrete sessions. The boundaries follow the ventilatory thresholds (VT1, VT2) and VO2max, and the volume split follows Seiler.
methodology.cogganText: 5-zone models, popularized in cycling by Andrew Coggan, often merge recovery and base endurance into a single zone and distinguish above-threshold work less finely. Zoned splits Z1/Z2 to keep recovery legible, and splits Z5/Z6 to separate VO2max from pure speed.
methodology.seilerText: Stephen Seiler groups training into three blocks: below the first ventilatory threshold (our Z1-Z2), between the two thresholds (our Z3, the "grey zone"), and above the second threshold (our Z4-Z6). It's the right level to steer a polarized split; Zoned adds sub-zones to write concrete sessions.
methodology.weekCaption: % of time run · teaching values, not a measurement from a real user.
methodology.weekNote: Z1+Z2 = easy · Z3 = grey zone · Z4→Z6 = hard

polarise.title: Why 80/20 works
polarise.seoDescription: What the research shows about training intensity distribution in endurance athletes, why the polarized model works, and its limits.
polarise.lede: Several studies on trained endurance athletes show the same thing: most of their volume is run very easily. That's not laziness — it's what makes the hard sessions possible.
polarise.measuredText1: Seiler reviewed the studies that track actual training distribution — via heart rate and lactate, not just stated intention — in trained endurance athletes. The pattern observed holds across disciplines: the large majority of sessions run below the first ventilatory threshold, a small share well above the second, and little time spent in between.
polarise.measuredText2: Stöggl and Sperlich then tested this distribution experimentally: over several weeks, a group of trained runners following a polarized distribution improved more on key endurance variables than a group training mostly at threshold, at high intensity, or at high moderate-intensity volume.
polarise.distributionCaption: Polarized volume split · rounded teaching values
polarise.whyText1: The adaptations that build endurance — capillary density, mitochondria, running economy — respond mostly to time spent running, not to intensity. Running it easily lets you accumulate a lot of it without a recovery debt.
polarise.whyText2: Conversely, threshold and VO2max work produces fast gains but costs a lot nervously. Two hard sessions a week, run genuinely hard because the rest was genuinely easy, beat four medium ones.
polarise.greyZoneText: The classic trap: running "reasonably fast" every day. Too hard to recover from, too easy to progress. Faude, Kindermann and Meyer show that the lactate threshold marks a narrow metabolic transition rather than a single point — sitting in it permanently keeps fatigue up without giving the clean stimulus of a real threshold session. That's why Zoned's Z3 is labelled "dose it".
polarise.change4hText: About 3 h 15 in Z1-Z2, 45 minutes in Z4-Z5: one hard session and one moderate-quality session.
polarise.change8hText: 6 h 30 in Z1-Z2, 1 h 30 hard. Easy volume grows, not the number of hard sessions.
polarise.changeText: This is the rule the plan generator follows: when you increase your volume, it adds easy running. When you cut it, it keeps the hard sessions and trims the easy ones.
limits: These studies look at trained athletes: at 3 h a week, dosing is a secondary question — running regularly is enough to progress.
80/20 is counted in sessions or time, not kilometres — the proportions change depending on the counting method.
Some race preparations (5K, cross-country, track) legitimately climb to 25-30% hard for a few weeks.
polarise.medicalDisclaimer: No medical advice. In case of pain or a medical condition, a health professional comes before any model.

paces.title: Where the paces come from
paces.seoDescription: Zoned's pace calibration in the open: one input, your MAS, the formula, the percentages per zone and what the model cannot know.
paces.heading: Where the paces come from
paces.intro: Zoned measures nothing about you. Every pace it displays — in sessions, in plans, in calculators — comes from a single figure you enter, your MAS, and from a percentage table published here in the open.
paces.formulaExample: MAS {{vma, number}} km/h · bottom of Z2, at {{pctSlow}} % of MAS → {{paceSlow}} min/km · top of Z2, at {{pctFast}} % → {{paceFast}} min/km.
paces.inputText: Your MAS, in km/h, is enough to compute every pace. Enter it directly, or estimate it from a recent race time with the MAS calculator. It stays in your browser.
paces.hrText: If you enter your max heart rate, Zoned derives a beat range per zone from it, with its own percentages. It complements pace, it does not replace it: the two scales do not line up exactly.
paces.tableNote: The ranges target the core of each zone: the margin left between two zones is deliberate. Z6 goes past 100 % of MAS, which is expected — those speeds only hold for seconds.
paces.raceText: Estimated race times start from the same MAS, with a percentage of their own per distance: the longer the race, the smaller the sustainable fraction of MAS. These are orders of magnitude for a runner trained for the distance, not a promise.
limits: Your MAS is already an estimate: two test protocols easily differ by a few tenths, which is several seconds per kilometre.
The percentages are an editorial choice grounded in the literature, not a lab measurement: other models cut the continuum differently.
The maths ignore terrain, elevation, heat, wind and how tired you are today: on those sessions, feel decides.
A zone pace is not a race target: estimated times assume training suited to the distance.

sources.title: Sources
sources.seoDescription: The scientific references Zoned cites: authors, year, journal, and what each one is used for in the app. No medical advice, open source.
sources.heading: {{count}} sources
sources.intro: All publicly accessible. Every zone and every pace guideline in Zoned rests on one of them; when a value is an editorial choice rather than a measurement, it's stated here.
sources.editorialChoiceText: Splitting into six zones rather than five or three
sources.editorialChoiceDetail: Zoned's editorial choice, not a measurement
sources.notMedicalText: Pain, a medical condition, pregnancy, return from injury: a health professional comes before any physiological model.
sources.notMeasureText: The paces and zones shown are estimates computed from what you entered. A lab test will say something different, and it will be right.
sources.notCoachText: Zoned doesn't see your fatigue, your sleep or your work week. It offers documented sessions; the judgment call stays yours.
sources.licenseText: The code, the data and the formulas used are in the public repository, in plain sight.

planMethodology.title: Plan Guide
planMethodology.seoDescription: The 7 evidence-based principles behind Zoned's training plan generation. Understand how your plan is built.
planMethodology.heading: How Zoned Builds Your Plan
planMethodology.intro: Every training plan in Zoned is generated from 7 evidence-based principles. No black box: here is exactly how your plan is built, and why.
planMethodology.introText: The plan generator combines periodization models from Daniels and Lydiard, the polarized training distribution validated by Seiler, volume progression rules derived from Gabbett's acute:chronic workload research, and the exponential taper model of Mujika & Padilla. Each parameter is adapted to your race distance, fitness level, and training goal.
planMethodology.introDisclaimer: These are the same principles used by professional coaches. The difference is that Zoned applies them automatically based on your profile.
